title: About me
text:
A little more about meAbout meI’m Steve, a researcher and engineer based in Brisbane. I work at QUT and co-founded Panalogy Lab, an independent applied AI research and development company.
    Engineering, economicsand a few turns along the wayMy background brings together electrical engineering, economics and hands-on project delivery. Before my current research and applied AI work, I worked on industrial automation, control systems, functional safety and multidisciplinary engineering projects.During my PhD in Economics, I studied how people and complex systems respond to change. My current work often brings the two backgrounds together: studying behaviour while building the software needed to investigate it.And yes, the moustache in this photo was for Movember, supporting men’s health during my engineering days.Engineering days, with a Movember moustache for men’s health.

title: Current research themes
text:
Behavioural economics · AI · Complex systemsCurrent research themesMy research examines how technologies, people and institutions evolve together. I use complexity science and behavioural economics to connect individual decisions, organisational change and wider social and economic outcomes.
    
      
        Current research themesHuman–AI interactionTechnology adoption & workKnowledge discoveryComplex systemsMethods & approaches
        Reach & collaborationCitations & readershipPolicy & public engagementResearch collaborations
        A complexity science of technological evolution: how individual behaviour, organisations and institutions shape—and are shaped by—technological change.
      
      
        01Human–AI interaction and evaluationHow well can generative AI represent human values, attitudes, preferences and decisions? I investigate synthetic populations, or silicon sampling, through comparisons with human evidence, sensitivity analysis and cross-model evaluation.This includes questions of cultural alignment, population heterogeneity, public opinion and organisational judgement. I’m interested in which research questions synthetic respondents can help address, and how to recognise the variation and uncertainty that their responses may miss.Selected workSurveyLM technical report ↗Comparing human and synthetic data in service research · Journal of Services Marketing ↗Using reminders with reward opportunities to reduce spectator no-show behavior · Journal of Business Research ↗AI prediction and human understanding · The Conversation ↗
        02Technology adoption, work and capabilityWhy do some workers and organisations adopt new technologies productively while others face barriers, risks or uneven benefits? I combine behavioural and institutional analysis with labour-market evidence, skill networks and models of adaptation.I led the Future Skills Organisation’s national study of generative AI adoption by Australian workers, engaging a working group spanning government, employers, unions and professional bodies. Current research extends these questions to occupational mobility, capability evolution, professional identity and the ways institutions shape technological change.Selected workNational AI adoption study & employer toolkit →AI and big data in sustainable entrepreneurship · Journal of Economic Surveys ↗AI copilots, work & professional identity →
        03Finding evidence in archives and interviewsI build research software for searching and analysing documents, archives and interviews. It combines semantic retrieval and language models with structured extraction and knowledge graphs, keeping results linked to the original material.Projects include historical Spanish Inquisition records, scientific interviews through Web of Stories, and AI-assisted qualitative analysis. Researchers need to be able to check what the software has extracted against the source.Selected workArchival research & scientometrics platforms →RiskWise AI-assisted qualitative analysis workflow →
        04Complex systems and behavioural economicsI study technological evolution as a complex adaptive process: people learn and make decisions, organisations develop capabilities, and institutions shape which changes persist. These micro, meso and macro levels influence one another through networks, feedback and adaptation.My PhD brought behavioural economics and complexity science together to study interacting agents and limited information. That perspective now informs my work on workforce transitions, AI, digital platforms, public health, financial markets and mobility.Selected workBridging Complexity and Behavioural Economics · PhD thesis ↗Artificial intelligence in the field of economics ↗Cognitive architectures for artificial intelligence ethics ↗
        How I workMethods & approachesI choose methods around the question, the scale of the system and the available evidence. That often means combining empirical analysis with computational models, then checking how sensitive the results are to the assumptions.Behaviour and evidence: surveys, experiments, behavioural economics, statistics and econometrics.Systems and structure: agent-based modelling, network analysis, scientometrics, geospatial and mobility analysis.AI and software: machine learning, model evaluation, retrieval-augmented generation, structured extraction and human review.My software work includes Python, R, Stata, MATLAB, SQL/PostgreSQL, Django REST Framework, React, Streamlit, API integration and AWS-hosted research applications.The Constrained Methods MatrixMy PhD thesis, Bridging Complexity and Behavioural Economics (QUT, 2023), developed a framework for choosing methods for complex problems. The Constrained Methods Matrix relates nine broad families of analytical methods to the number of causes involved, the scale of their effects, and the complexity and uncertainty of the information available.The framework grew out of work with Professor Benno Torgler, building on ideas from Marvin Minsky, Aaron Sloman and Push Singh. Its boundaries are deliberately soft: statistical, qualitative and case-based reasoning may be useful together, and collecting different data can make other approaches feasible.I also consider feedback between levels of a system. Individual behaviour can change an organisation, while organisational rules shape what individuals can do; these effects unfold at different speeds. The relevant focal level might be a workplace, a sector or a region.View the methods matrix and feedback diagramView larger ↗Figure 1 · The Constrained Methods Matrix, extended version. Thesis p. 13, adapted from Bickley & Torgler (2023). Thesis and source context ↗View larger ↗Figure 5 · Nested feedback loops. Thesis p. 56. The chapter draws on hierarchical systems work by Simon (1962) and Ceddia et al. (2013). Thesis and source context ↗In the thesis, I applied this perspective to public health, financial markets, mobility and the development of AI. Read the complete thesis ↗
        Research reachCitations and readershipMy work is read across economics, AI, public health and related fields. title: Hi, I’m Steve.
text:
Researcher · Engineer · Entrepreneur
        Hi, I’m Steve.
        I study how people and technology shape one another.
        I’m Dr Steve J. Bickley, a Brisbane-based researcher and engineer working across applied AI, behavioural economics and complex systems.
        At QUT and ARC BITA, I explore how people make decisions, adopt technology and adapt to change. As co-founder of Panalogy Lab, I also help turn research into useful software and industrial applications.

Teaching, supervision & sharingTeaching and supervisionI teach economics and research methods. In class, I use worked examples and demonstrations to connect a method’s assumptions with the questions it can help answer.
    
      Learning & communityUniversity teachingOpen research resourcesSupervision & mentoringNudgeathon communityInvited speaking & panelsInterested in research training or supervision? Get in touch.
      
        Queensland University of TechnologyUniversity teachingEFB350 · Data Capture and Research DesignCo-Developer, Co-Coordinator & Lecturer · Undergraduate · 2024–2025I helped develop and deliver a 13-week interdisciplinary unit informed by the methods framework from my doctoral research. Students explored experimental and survey design, narrative and content analysis, networks, agent-based modelling, biosensors, remote sensing, online data collection and generative AI.Practical activities connected research principles with R, Qualtrics/SMARTRIQs, LIWC-22, Gephi, NetLogo, Python and AI APIs.         Workshops and open resourcesSharing research toolsARC BITA Geek Seminar SeriesI co-founded and coordinate this practical seminar series on empirical methods and technologies for behavioural insights and technology adoption. I developed and maintain its public GitHub knowledge hub, preserving slides, code demonstrations, recordings where available and further reading.Browse the knowledge hub ↗“Synthetic Data Generation and Silicon Sampling Using Augmented Language Models”I designed and delivered a five-part ARC BITA research-skills workshop series in May–October 2024, covering synthetic respondents, language-model-based research, experimental design, evaluation and responsible use.“How Can I Use AI to Help My Academic Research?”My invited University of Western Australia lecture in April 2025, “How Can I Use AI to Help My Academic Research?”, brought together more than 120 participants in person and online.Augmented language models workshop materials ↗AI for academic research: slides, recording and examples ↗
        Research developmentSupervision and mentoringMy supervision spans applied AI, behavioural economics, computational methods, information systems and technology adoption. Depending on the project, I help with study design and analysis, computational models or software, and preparing the work for publication.As of October 2026, I have held eight Associate Supervisor appointments, including an MPhil candidate who completed in August 2026 and subsequently progressed to doctoral study.I support domestic and international researchers from different disciplinary backgrounds. As of October 2026, the cohort includes four women and four international candidates.I also mentor research assistants, software developers and undergraduate researchers. My QUT Vacation Research Experience Scheme (VRES) supervision includes three students across the 2023/24 and 2024/25 intakes, with three further students in the 2026/27 intake. I have also mentored six Year 11 students through Mansfield State High School’s Digital Solutions Mentorship Program during 2024–2026.I’m open to enquiries from prospective MPhil and PhD students at QUT, and to joint supervision with colleagues at other Australian and international universities, subject to institutional arrangements. Get in touch about supervision →
        Behavioural science, togetherThe Nudgeathon communityNudgeathon is an annual behavioural science competition where teams of students, government officials and industry professionals tackle real-world social and policy challenges. It has been part of my journey from student competitor to mentor and coach. As a coach, I help teams work through the behavioural evidence and the practical limits of their proposals.
